description: We are a passionate team of young innovators from Kodland’s Python PRO course, eager to turn code into real-world impact. Driven by a shared curiosity for technology and space, we are stepping up to the NASA Space Apps Challenge to put our skills in advanced programming, problem-solving, and software development into practice. Under the mentorship and organization of Professor Arthur Morgado Teixeira, our team is ready to code and build creative solutions for the universe's toughest challenges!
summary:
Humanity’s Future Is Red is a browser-based game where kids plan and run a Mars outpost using real NASA mission data. In the planning phase, players choose a landing site, a launch architecture from NASA’s Mars Design Reference Architecture 5.0 (nuclear thermal or chemical), surface modules and crew size. In the survival phase, they make three decisions per sol (Martian day), and every decision costs something: oxygen, water, food, power, habitat integrity or crew stress. There is no free choice.
The game is also an open platform. Events and modules are plain data, so teachers, students and other developers can write new situations with their own real-world basis and add them to the game without rebuilding it. Every event carries a badge (“Real NASA event”, “Real NASA data” or “Inspired by NASA data”) with the source and a link, so players know which part is real.
It matters because kids see how mission planners actually think, not only how missions end. And because anyone can add new events, the game can keep up with new NASA findings.
details:
Phase 1, Mission planning. The player picks one of four landing sites: Jezero Crater, Arcadia Planitia, Gale Crater or Valles Marineris. Each has its own solar efficiency, dust wear, access to subsurface water ice, natural radiation shielding, science multiplier and science objectives. The player then picks one of two rocket architectures (Ares V with a nuclear thermal rocket at 900 s Isp, or Ares V chemical with aerocapture at 450 s Isp). Next come the surface modules (solar array, water recycler, plant habitat and MOXIE oxygen production), crew size and mission length. A “Mission Telemetry” sidebar shows the effect of every choice live: payload mass against the rocket’s limit, power balance, consumables and daily radiation dose. The trip itself consumes resources, so the rocket choice carries over into the survival phase.

Phase 2, Survival. Each sol has a morning, afternoon and night decision. When the night decision is made, the sol closes and daily consumption and wear are deducted. Two dashboards track the outpost: Life Support (oxygen, water, food, power, crew stress) and Structure & Science (habitat integrity, samples and science points). The score is science points, so the player has to keep the crew alive and the outpost working to earn them.

The trade-off engine

Every event has a “yes” and a “no” option, and both have a cost. The chosen option’s effects always apply. The option can also carry a risk: the game rolls a chance of an “incident” on top. The crew’s stress changes the odds. A stressed crew makes more mistakes (incident chances grow by up to 50%) and produces less science (up to 40% less). That ties the human side of the mission to the numbers: pushing the crew for science today makes tomorrow’s incidents more likely. Events can also temporarily drain or save power for several sols. This is why a choice that saves oxygen today can cost power tomorrow.

The idea, the game design (two phases, three decisions per sol, a cost on every choice, the stress mechanic, the open event and module system) and the selection of NASA sources are ours. We used SI tools to speed up the work:

Custom events and modules

  • Events. The catalogue of 32 situations is a data file with a simple builder. An event declares its period of the day, the sites where it can happen, the conditions it requires (such as a module being equipped, or oxygen below a threshold), scheduled or urgent triggers, the effects of each option, and its optional risk. A built-in validator checks new events, so a mistake in a custom event is caught before it reaches players.
  • Real-world basis. Each event can carry its own NASA record: the kind (real event, real data or analog), a fact written in our own words, the source and a link. This is how new events inherit the game’s transparency.
  • Modules. Modules are entries in a data table (mass, power draw, whether they generate power, pros and cons) that feed straight into the telemetry and the mass and power budgets.
  • Benefit. A teacher can build a lesson around a specific mission event (for example, a dust storm) by writing one entry, with no changes to the game engine.

Replayability. Four sites, two rockets, module combinations, random event order and chance-based incidents change every run. The crew of each run is drawn at random from a pool of real astronauts. Rank titles from “Rookie Outpost” to “Mars Observatory” give players a goal to beat next time.

Accessibility. The game runs in the browser with no download or account. Terms like sol are explained in context, and each situation is written in plain language.

What we hope to achieve. We want a player to finish a run understanding at least one true constraint of deep space survival, and to be curious enough to open the real NASA source behind it. We also want the event and module system to let the game grow with the community.

Tools used. Python and Flask on the backend (the game logic, data and validator), JavaScript and React on the front-end, HTML and CSS.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

  • Code: Gemini and Claude helped write the first draft of the code, mainly the front-end. The team reviewed, tested and adapted the code.
  • Sprites and images: PixelLab, Grok and Gemini were used to generate pixel-art sprites.
  • Audio: ElevenLabs was used for voice dubbing.
  • Data verification: ChatPDF was used to analyze and check data in the NASA documents. The team checked the figures against the original sources.
  • Text: Gemini and Claude helped revise texts, including this report.
